nameStory: The orange-legged furrow bee gets its colorful name from the bright orange or reddish legs that distinguish it from many other sweat bees. The 'furrow' part refers to the grooved lines that run across the bee's abdomen, creating distinctive striped patterns that look like tiny plowed fields.
description: The orange-legged furrow bee is a small, metallic sweat bee about the size of a honeybee worker, typically measuring around 10-12mm long. These bees have a dark, often greenish-bronze body with a subtle metallic sheen and distinctive orange to reddish-brown legs. Like other sweat bees, they're attracted to human perspiration for its salt content, though they're gentle and rarely sting unless handled roughly. They're actually non-native bees that arrived in North America long ago, crossing the ancient Bering land bridge during the ice ages.

idTips.label: Orange legs
idTips.description: Look for bright orange to reddish-brown legs that stand out against the dark body - this is the most reliable field mark and much more vivid than the pale legs of most other sweat bees

idTips.label: Metallic body
idTips.description: The body has a dark greenish-bronze or blackish color with a subtle metallic sheen that catches the light, feeling smooth and hard to the touch if handled

idTips.label: Furrowed abdomen
idTips.description: The abdomen shows distinct grooved lines or furrows running across it, creating a striped appearance that feels slightly ridged under magnification

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: About honeybee-sized but more compact and robust, with a rounded body that appears less fuzzy than most other bees

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with quick, darting movements close to the ground, often hovering near flowers or landing frequently on bare soil

habitat: Orange-legged furrow bees prefer areas with exposed soil for nesting, including gardens, parks, field edges, and disturbed ground throughout New England. They're commonly found in sunny locations with diverse flowering plants, from sea level to moderate elevations. Look for them in areas where bare patches of well-drained soil meet flowering plants like asters, goldenrod, and garden flowers.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge in late spring, with females beginning to excavate ground nests in bare soil. Early spring flowers like dandelions and fruit tree blossoms attract the first generation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with both solitary females and social colonies active. Most easily observed visiting a wide variety of flowers throughout the day, especially in sunny weather.
seasonality.fall: Second generation adults are active on late-season flowers like asters and goldenrod. Mated females prepare to overwinter while males die off after mating.
seasonality.winter: Adults are dormant, overwintering in protected locations. Only mated females survive the cold months, emerging to start new colonies the following spring.

funFact: This bee is a social shape-shifter - in cold climates with short summers, orange-legged furrow bees live completely alone, but in warmer areas they form cooperative colonies with queens and workers, sometimes with both lifestyles happening in the same neighborhood!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other dark sweat bees, but the bright orange legs are a dead giveaway - most other sweat bees have pale yellow, brown, or dark legs. Memory trick: 'Orange legs, furrow bee' - it's really that simple!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sweat bees,' these insects are actually beneficial pollinators that are only mildly interested in human sweat for its salt content. They're much less aggressive than their name might suggest and play important roles in pollinating both wild plants and garden flowers.
compareHints: Among the furrow bees, orange-legged furrow bees are distinguished by their bright orange legs, while ligated furrow bees have pale legs and more pronounced white abdominal bands. The confusing furrow bee lives up to its name by being very similar, but typically has darker, less orange-tinted legs and slightly different furrow patterns on the abdomen.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Ligated Furrow Bee can be distinguished from its close relatives by its consistent dark metallic coloration and widespread abundance — it's the most commonly observed furrow bee in New England with over 6,000 recorded sightings.
Compared to the Ligated Furrow Bee, the Confusing Furrow Bee tends to have a more bronze (less greenish) metallic sheen.
Unlike the Ligated Furrow Bee which has more irregular banding, the Parallel-striped Sweat Bee has distinctly even, parallel stripes.
